name: Social Hierarchy, Slavery, and Patronage

objectives.text: Identify the servant and the master in a Bible story such as Jesus healing the centurion's servant
Recall from Scripture that God made both rich people and poor people
Retell how Jesus washed his disciples' feet, a job usually done by a servant
Describe the main social groups of the Roman world, including senators, wealthy landowners, citizens, freed people, and slaves
Explain what Roman citizenship meant and how Paul used his citizenship when he was arrested
Describe how people became slaves in the Roman world and the kinds of work slaves did
Retell the story of Onesimus and explain what Paul asked Philemon to do for him
Describe how the first believers in Jerusalem shared their goods so that no one among them was in need
Describe the structure of a Roman household, including the head of the household, family members, and slaves, and explain why whole households joined the church together
Contrast Jesus' teaching on greatness through service with the way Roman rulers exercised authority
Explain how honor and shame shaped social life in the Roman world and identify examples in the Gospels
Analyze the patron and client system of gifts, loyalty, and obligation in Roman society
Explain how Jesus' instruction to invite those who cannot repay challenged the expectations of patronage
Interpret Paul's statement that there is neither slave nor free in Christ within its first-century setting
Explain how divisions between rich and poor at Corinthian church meals led Paul to rebuke their practice of the Lord's Supper
Apply James' warning against favoring the rich to a first-century scene of seating in a gathering of believers
Explain why Paul reminded the Corinthians that not many of them were wise, powerful, or of noble birth
Compare Roman slavery with race-based chattel slavery in American history, identifying both differences and shared injustices
Identify women of means who acted as patrons of Jesus and the early church, such as Phoebe, Lydia, and the women of Luke 8, and explain their role
Analyze how New Testament writers used the language of slavery, purchase, and freedom to describe redemption in Christ
Analyze the New Testament household codes in their Roman context, noting how they address slaves as moral agents and place duties on masters
Explain the significance of Christ taking the form of a slave and dying by crucifixion, a punishment associated with slaves
Compare the Roman ideal of benefaction that expected a return with the New Testament teaching of grace given freely
Evaluate how Paul's teaching in Philemon, his counsel to gain freedom, and his condemnation of enslavers undermined the foundations of slavery
Evaluate how defenders of slavery and abolitionists in American history used the household codes, judging which reading fits the text in its context
Compose an essay explaining how the early church formed a community across lines of status, wealth, and citizenship, drawing on Scripture and the Reformed confession of the communion of saints

changes: Kept and sharpened real competencies on masters and servants, citizenship, Roman slavery, Onesimus, patronage, Galatians 3:28, the Lord's Supper, women in society, the Roman household, slavery's undermining, and church sociology, anchoring each to verses. Replaced vague early items (rich and poor, Jesus loves everyone) with text-based ones (Proverbs 22:2, foot washing). Dropped the belief-oriented and vague comparisons in favor of specific analyses. Added honor and shame, Luke 14 and patronage, James 2 partiality, 1 Corinthians 1 status, women patrons, redemption metaphors, household codes in context, Christ as slave, grace versus benefaction, comparison with American slavery, and historical use of the household codes, with confessional anchors in WCF 26, Heidelberg Q55, and WLC Q129, Q130, and Q142.
